newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia warms to security summit idea, U.S. cool.
newsitem.headline: Russia warms to security summit idea, U.S. cool.

text.p: Russia said on Thursday it was ready to take part in a five-power summit on European security, but a frosty U.S. response to the idea cast doubts on whether such a meeting could go ahead.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said the idea of the summit had been floated at meetings with Western leaders.
"The question of a meeting of the "Big Five" this spring arose at meetings in Moscow," Interfax news agency quoted him as saying.

"The main thing for us is the question of the content of this meeting and of its careful preparation. As a result of the meeting we would have to find our way to a realistic result that would suit everyone."

Both French President Jacques Chirac and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl have visited Russia this year and diplomats said on Wednesday that they backed the idea of a security summit, suggested for April.

Such a meeting, bringing together the United States, Britain, France and Germany, would allow Russia to discuss NATO plans to expand eastwards before NATO holds its own decisive summit on the issue this summer.
Moscow is bitterly opposed to NATO expansion, arguing that it would threaten domestic security and that it could undermine the already shaky political position of President Boris Yeltsin.
But many Russian officials accept privately that expansion will go ahead. "Nobody in the Russian leadership thinks it will be possible to stop NATO expansion. It's only words," said one.

Yeltsin's opponents in the State Duma, the lower house of parliament, argue that Yeltsin, who had open heart surgery in early November and now is recovering slowly from pneumonia, is not well enough to rule Russia.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, currently holding talks with U.S. Vice-President Al Gore in Washington, has said he thinks a planned summit between Yeltsin and U.S. President Bill Clinton should be moved from the United States to Europe to conserve Yeltsin's strength.
But U.S. officials said they had not promoted the security summit idea, which could also provide a forum for bilateral talks between Yeltsin and Clinton.
"We asked the French about the press reports and I don't believe that any such proposal will be forthcoming," a senior U.S. official, speaking on condition he was not named, said.

"There's a concern among the smaller countries in NATO that this historic decision, which is arguably the most important decision NATO will have made since its creation, not be made in two or three places."
NATO is expected to issue invitations at a summit in Madrid this summer. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are expected to be the first new members.
The Western alliance has made clear that enlargement will go ahead, although it wants to take account of Russia's fears and does not want to alienate Moscow.
Chernomyrdin said this week that it would be hard to explain NATO expansion to the Russian people.
"We are all members of the post-war generation and NATO was our enemy for 50 years," he said in a television interview.
"We were told that NATO was our enemy and suddenly NATO is approaching our borders."
